newsitem.title: CROATIA: Tudjman illness may leave Croatian power vacuum.
newsitem.headline: Tudjman illness may leave Croatian power vacuum.

text.p: Croatian President Franjo Tudjman rules with an iron fist and his illness may leave a power vacuum that could easily cause instability in the newborn Balkan democracy, analysts say.
The 74-year old president could not have chosen a worse moment to fall ill, they believe.
His personal popularity is declining, his ruling party is quarrelling, the opposition is boycotting parliament and key presidential and local elections are looming.
"If Tudjman disappears from the scene Croatia will find itself in a very embarrassing political situation," analyst Davor Gjenero told Reuters.
Tudjman's ruling Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) party is reeling from corruption scandals and faction power struggles, with only his "Father of the Nation" figure keeping it together.

There is no one in Tudjman's shadow to inherit the position of the leader of the 4.7-million nation that five years ago parted from communist Yugoslavia to win independence for the first time since the 11th century.
"The ruling party has no common political idea binding them, they have no second man who has something to offer," Gjenero said in a telephone interview.

Defence Minister Gojko Susak, informal leader of the powerful Bosnian Croat lobby from Herzegovina, is de facto "number two" and favourite of the party, which is becoming more hardline since taking over power in 1990.
Susak is the only person who could control hardline separatist Croats from western Herzegovina, who are a major threat to the Dayton peace agreement that ended the 43-months old Bosnian war.
But he too is seriously ill -- he was treated in the U.S. last year for lung cancer.
Other popular politicians, like the moderate Foreign Minister Mate Granic, have a weak power base within the HDZ.
Under the Constitution, the Speaker of the Parliament, currently Vlatko Pavletic would take over Tudjman's responsibilities in case the president was judged incapacitated by the Supreme Court.
"It is unclear now what would happen (if Tudjman is unable to perform his duties)," an opposition leader Stjepo Martinovic told Reuters.

"But in any case it would be good for Croatia because Tudjman's regime has led Croatia into a blind alley...it would be excellent if people who are really capable of leading the country came to power," he said.
But analysts believe the chances of the opposition taking power are minimal, given its disunity, lack of money and lack of control over the media.
